stem: You are the resident covering the wards overnight at a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide. The physician is available by phone. At 22:30 the nurse asks you to see a 32-year-old Aboriginal man admitted two days ago with lower-leg cellulitis. He has had 48 hours of intravenous flucloxacillin, is afebrile with observations in the normal range, and the erythema is receding behind the marked line. He has just learned that his uncle has died in Port Augusta and tells you he must leave tonight to travel there for Sorry Business. He is calm and clearly understands that his infection is not yet fully treated. He has a mobile phone and family will drive him.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Explain that he must remain until the intravenous course is finished and document that he was advised not to leave tonight
Acknowledge his obligation, review for oral antibiotics and arrange Port Augusta follow-up agreed with the physician
Ask him to sign the discharge against medical advice form so that he can leave tonight without further delay
Suggest that his family travel to the hospital instead, so that he can grieve here while completing his treatment

explanations.A: Insisting he stay ignores a cultural obligation that is central to his wellbeing and his standing in his community. He has capacity and will leave regardless; the doctor's job is to make that departure as safe as possible, not to refuse to plan for it.
explanations.B: Attending Sorry Business is a recognised cultural obligation, not an inconvenience. He is clinically improving and meets usual criteria for intravenous-to-oral switch, so a planned early discharge on oral antibiotics with a review arranged through an Aboriginal health service near where he will be, written instructions on return precautions and a brief phone call to the physician on call is the safest and most culturally responsive plan.
explanations.C: Treating this as discharge against medical advice frames a reasonable decision as non-compliance and often ends with no antibiotics, no follow-up and no handover. The form does not remove the duty to arrange safe ongoing care.
explanations.D: Asking the family to come to him misunderstands Sorry Business, which involves travelling to be with community for ceremony; it is not something that can be relocated to the ward.

learning_point: When a patient must leave for Sorry Business, plan a safe early discharge (oral switch, follow-up near their destination, return advice) rather than framing the departure as non-compliance.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without an on-site Aboriginal Liaison Officer overnight, the resident may need to make the follow-up arrangements directly, contacting the Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service or hospital at the destination town and handing over by phone; in a tertiary hospital the Aboriginal Liaison Officer or Aboriginal Health Practitioner would usually coordinate this.
learning_area: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Cellulitis and erysipelas; intravenous to oral switch

references.title: SA Health Aboriginal Health Care Framework and Aboriginal Patient Pathway Officer guidance

tutor_context: Key facts: Sorry Business describes the period of mourning and the ceremonial and family obligations following a death; attending is a serious obligation. Cellulitis improving after 48 hours of intravenous therapy in an afebrile patient meets usual oral-switch criteria. Common misconception: that a patient who leaves before planned completion of therapy must be processed as discharge against medical advice. Out of scope: specific antibiotic choice and dosing for the oral switch, and the hospital's leave-of-absence paperwork.
plan: Tests the decision to plan a safe early discharge around a cultural obligation instead of framing it as non-compliance (outcomes 1.3, 3.3, 3.6). Patient is improving cellulitis in a Mid North hospital overnight with physician by phone. Distractors: insist he stays (paternalistic, ignores capacity), DAMA form (abdicates follow-up), relocate the family (misunderstands Sorry Business). Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines oral-switch criteria and SA Health Aboriginal health care guidance.

stem: You are the PGY2 on the general ward of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide. The visiting physician has reviewed a 19-year-old Aboriginal woman admitted two days ago with community-acquired pneumonia and has agreed she can go home tomorrow. She has known rheumatic heart disease with moderate mitral regurgitation and is prescribed 4-weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin as secondary prophylaxis; the medication chart and the hospital record show her last injection was seven weeks ago, and she says the clinic she usually attends has closed. She has no current GP, her last echocardiogram was 10 months ago and she mentions she is overdue for a dental check. You have a long task list before the end of the day.
lead_in: Which task is the most important to complete before she leaves hospital?

options.text: Book an outpatient dental check-up for her through the regional public dental health service
Request a follow-up chest X-ray in six weeks' time to confirm that her pneumonia has fully resolved
Give the overdue benzathine benzylpenicillin today and notify the rheumatic heart disease register
Arrange her next surveillance echocardiogram for 12 months after her previous echocardiogram

explanations.A: Dental health matters in rheumatic heart disease because of endocarditis risk, but a routine dental review can be organised after discharge; it does not carry the immediate risk that a lapse in secondary prophylaxis does.
explanations.B: Follow-up imaging after pneumonia is reasonable in selected patients but is a low-urgency task that can be requested through her future GP.
explanations.C: Each missed or late benzathine benzylpenicillin dose exposes her to recurrence of acute rheumatic fever, which worsens valve damage; she is already three weeks overdue. Giving the dose in hospital today and informing the rheumatic heart disease register and control program, so they can re-establish her recall and link her to a new clinic, is the highest-value action and is within a PGY2's scope.
explanations.D: Echocardiographic surveillance is important but is not due for another two months; it can be requested in the discharge plan rather than before she leaves.

learning_point: For a patient with rheumatic heart disease, maintaining secondary benzathine benzylpenicillin prophylaxis and keeping the rheumatic heart disease register informed takes priority over routine surveillance tasks.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the resident may be the only clinician who notices the lapse; the SA Rheumatic Heart Disease Control Program can be contacted directly to re-establish recall and identify a local clinic or Aboriginal health service that can give ongoing injections.
learning_area: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health
presentation: acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease

references.title: The 2020 Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease (RHDAustralia)
references.locator: Secondary prophylaxis; register and control programs

references.title: SA Health Rheumatic Heart Disease Control Program

tutor_context: Key facts: secondary prophylaxis with benzathine benzylpenicillin every 4 weeks (or 3-weekly in selected high-risk patients) is the single most effective intervention to prevent recurrence and progression of rheumatic heart disease; adherence above about 80 percent of doses is needed. Hospital admission is an opportunity to give an overdue dose. SA has an RHD register and control program under the Public Health Act notification system. Common misconception: that prophylaxis is managed by the register and is not the admitting team's concern. Out of scope: anticoagulation and surgical timing for valve disease.
plan: Tests prioritisation: among several reasonable discharge tasks, closing the gap in secondary prophylaxis and informing the register is the one that cannot wait (outcomes 1.3, 4.4, 2.8). Patient is a young Aboriginal woman with RHD admitted for pneumonia in a Mid North hospital. Distractors are all legitimate but lower-urgency surveillance tasks. Supported by the 2020 Australian ARF/RHD guideline.

stem: You are the intern on the surgical ward of a regional hospital that has a small medical ward without intensive care, CT during business hours only and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. A 38-year-old Aboriginal man has been admitted for incision and drainage of a thigh abscess under the visiting surgeon tomorrow morning. He is afebrile and well hydrated, with blood pressure 152/94 mmHg. His admission bloods show creatinine 148 micromol/L, eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m2, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, HbA1c 8.9 percent and a urine albumin-creatinine ratio of 42 mg/mmol. The state pathology record shows an eGFR of 55 and albumin-creatinine ratio of 38 from a presentation 7 months ago. He has not seen a GP since. The anaesthetist has asked you to summarise his renal function for the pre-operative note.
lead_in: Which interpretation of these results is most accurate?

options.text: Acute kidney injury from the abscess and sepsis, expected to recover with intravenous fluids over the next 48 hours
Renal function within the expected range for a man of his age, with no implications for his peri-operative care
Nephrotic syndrome from an undiagnosed glomerulonephritis, requiring urgent transfer to Adelaide for renal biopsy
Chronic kidney disease stage 3a with moderately increased albuminuria, most likely from diabetic kidney disease

explanations.A: Acute kidney injury cannot be assumed when a similar eGFR and albuminuria were documented seven months earlier; he is also afebrile and well hydrated, so a pre-renal cause is unlikely.
explanations.B: An eGFR of 52 in a 38-year-old is not normal, and albuminuria of 42 mg/mmol confirms kidney damage. Dismissing it would miss a treatable, progressive disease and the chance to avoid peri-operative harm.
explanations.C: Nephrotic syndrome requires heavy proteinuria (albumin-creatinine ratio typically above 220 mg/mmol) with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema; his albuminuria is moderate and there is no indication for urgent biopsy.
explanations.D: Reduced eGFR (45 to 59) with albuminuria of 3 to 30 mg/mmol or more persisting over at least three months meets the definition of chronic kidney disease; with his HbA1c and blood pressure the likely cause is diabetic kidney disease. Recognising this changes peri-operative prescribing (avoid NSAIDs, dose-adjust renally cleared drugs, maintain hydration) and must trigger follow-up, ideally through a GP or Aboriginal health service, with renal referral criteria applied.

learning_point: A reduced eGFR with albuminuria on two occasions more than three months apart means chronic kidney disease, which changes peri-operative prescribing and demands planned follow-up.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the renal unit is in Adelaide, so the intern should document the finding clearly for the GP and discuss referral thresholds with the visiting physician; telehealth nephrology review is often available.
learning_area: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

references.title: Kidney Health Australia, Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) Management in Primary Care (5th edition)
references.locator: Diagnosis and staging of CKD; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic

tutor_context: Key facts: CKD is defined as eGFR below 60 or evidence of kidney damage (albuminuria) persisting for at least 3 months; staging uses both eGFR and albuminuria categories. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults have roughly twice the prevalence of CKD and much higher rates of kidney failure, and Kidney Health Australia recommends kidney health checks from age 18 in this population. Common misconception: labelling every abnormal creatinine on admission as acute kidney injury. Out of scope: initiating SGLT2 inhibitors or ACE inhibitors from the surgical ward.
plan: Tests interpretation of eGFR and albuminuria over time as chronic kidney disease and its peri-operative implications (outcomes 1.5, 4.4, 1.8). Patient is a young Aboriginal man on a regional surgical ward with prior comparable results in the state record. Distractors: AKI (ignores prior results), normal variant (dangerous dismissal), nephrotic syndrome (misreads albuminuria magnitude). Supported by Kidney Health Australia CKD management handbook.

stem: You are the PGY2 on a general medical ward of a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. On the morning ward round the team reviews a 31-year-old Aboriginal woman from a remote community who was admitted overnight with pyelonephritis. She is clinically improving. During the review she looks at the floor, gives brief answers, and says "yeah" when the registrar asks whether she understands that she will need to stay for intravenous antibiotics and whether she has any questions. Afterwards the registrar remarks that she seems "disengaged and probably won't comply" and asks you to document that she has been counselled and agrees with the plan. The ward's Aboriginal Liaison Officer has not yet been told she is an inpatient.
lead_in: Which interpretation of her responses is most appropriate?

options.text: Her brief answers may reflect communication norms or feeling unsafe, so her understanding and agreement cannot be assumed
Her responses show she understands the plan and consents to it, so documenting her agreement is appropriate
Her quiet presentation most likely indicates depression, and a mental health assessment should be requested
Her lack of engagement suggests intoxication or withdrawal, which should be assessed before any further discussion with her

explanations.A: For many Aboriginal people, direct eye contact and extended conversation with unfamiliar authority figures on a crowded ward round are uncomfortable, and "yeah" may be a polite acknowledgement rather than informed agreement. The safe approach is to return later, sit with her, use open questions and allow silence, offer the Aboriginal Liaison Officer, and ask about family involvement before documenting that she understands.
explanations.B: Documenting agreement on the basis of a monosyllabic reply during a team ward round risks recording consent that was never truly given, which is both a communication failure and a documentation error.
explanations.C: Depression is a possible contributor in any inpatient but there is nothing here to support it over the more likely explanation; leaping to a psychiatric label is itself a form of bias.
explanations.D: There is no clinical information suggesting intoxication or withdrawal; attributing a quiet manner to substance use is a stereotype that contributes to inequitable care.

learning_point: Quiet, brief answers from an Aboriginal patient during a ward round are not evidence of understanding, agreement or disengagement; check understanding one-to-one, with the Aboriginal Liaison Officer and family where wanted.
setting_note: In a tertiary hospital the Aboriginal Liaison Officer service is usually available each weekday and should be notified of every Aboriginal inpatient; in a regional hospital the resident may need to call the Aboriginal health team or a local Aboriginal health service directly.
learning_area: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

references.title: National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards (2nd edition), User guide for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health
Medical Board of Australia, Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia
references.locator: Section 4.7 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health and cultural safety

tutor_context: Key facts: cultural safety is defined by the patient's experience, not the clinician's intent. Gratuitous concurrence (agreeing to be polite or to end an uncomfortable exchange) is well described. Good practice includes introducing yourself, sitting down, open questions, comfortable silence, asking who she wants involved, and notifying the Aboriginal Liaison Officer on admission. Common misconception: that labels like "non-compliant" are clinical observations rather than judgements. Out of scope: antibiotic choice for pyelonephritis.
plan: Tests interpretation of a communication style through a culturally safe lens and the risk of documenting assumed consent (outcomes 1.3, 3.4, 1.2). Scene is a tertiary ward round with a registrar primed to label the patient. Distractors: accept the agreement at face value, medicalise as depression, stereotype as substance use. Supported by the ACSQHC Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander user guide and Good medical practice section 4.7.

stem: You are the junior doctor on the surgical ward of a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre; overnight you cover the ward and the emergency department alone, with the surgeon on call by phone. A 56-year-old Aboriginal man is day one after an open appendicectomy. When you ask how he is, he says he is "alright" and does not ask for anything. The nurse tells you he has not got out of bed, grimaces when he moves, has declined the charted oxycodone twice and has not eaten. His nephew, who is visiting, says quietly that "Uncle won't complain, he never does". Observations are normal apart from a heart rate of 102 beats per minute.
lead_in: Which interpretation of this situation is most appropriate?

options.text: He is experiencing little pain, and his analgesia can now be stepped down to paracetamol alone
He is declining opioids because of a probable history of substance misuse that should be clarified
His answer may understate his pain, which should be assessed by function, behaviour and a suitable scale
His nephew is influencing his answers and so should be asked to leave the room during clinical assessments

explanations.A: Immobility, grimacing, poor intake and tachycardia all point to uncontrolled pain despite the reassuring words; stepping down analgesia would compound the problem and raise his risk of complications such as atelectasis and venous thromboembolism.
explanations.B: There is nothing in the history to suggest substance misuse. Assuming it is a stereotype; the more likely reasons for declining are stoicism, not wanting to be a bother, concern about what the tablets are for, or previous experience of being dismissed.
explanations.C: Under-reporting of pain is common and may reflect stoicism, cultural norms around men's health, mistrust or unfamiliarity with hospital routines. Observing behaviour and function, using a pain tool he can relate to, explaining what the medication is and why it will help him recover, and involving his nephew if he wishes gives a truer picture and better care.
explanations.D: The nephew is offering useful insight and his presence is likely to make the patient feel safer; excluding family undermines trust and is contrary to culturally safe practice.

learning_point: A patient who says he is "alright" but shows behavioural and physiological signs of pain needs his pain assessed by function and observation, not accepted at face value.
setting_note: In a country hospital there is usually no acute pain service and no on-site Aboriginal Liaison Officer overnight, so the junior doctor and nursing staff carry the assessment themselves and should document their approach for the morning team.
learning_area: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic
National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards, User guide for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health
references.locator: Partnering with consumers; culturally safe care

tutor_context: Key facts: self-report is the gold standard for pain but must be elicited in a way the patient trusts; behavioural indicators (guarding, immobility, poor intake) and physiological signs (tachycardia) support the assessment. Family and the Aboriginal Liaison Officer can help a patient express needs. Common misconception: that declining opioids signals misuse. Out of scope: opioid dosing and multimodal regimen details.
plan: Tests interpretation of under-reported post-operative pain in an Aboriginal man and the role of family (outcomes 1.3, 3.6, 1.4). Scene is a country surgical ward overnight. Distractors: accept "alright" and de-escalate, stereotype about substance misuse, exclude the nephew. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines pain assessment and the ACSQHC Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander user guide.

stem: You are the PGY2 on a busy medical ward of a metropolitan general hospital, with a registrar on site overnight. You are making a planned telehealth follow-up call to a 20-year-old Aboriginal man who left the ward two days ago, before completing intravenous antibiotics for a leg cellulitis, after signing a discharge against medical advice form. He explains that he had to go home to look after his younger siblings. The leg is still red and sore but he is not febrile. He asks whether he is "still allowed" to come back to the hospital, or whether he has to go somewhere else now because he signed the form.
lead_in: Which statement correctly describes his entitlement to care after a discharge against medical advice?

options.text: The signed form ends the hospital's duty of care, so he must now present to a general practitioner or a different hospital
His right to care and the hospital's duty of care continue unchanged, and he can return to this hospital at any time
He may return only if he is formally readmitted under the original consultant and agrees to complete the intravenous course
Because he left with an untreated infection, he can be detained under the Mental Health Act 2009 if he refuses to return

explanations.A: A discharge against medical advice form documents that risks were explained; it does not waive the patient's entitlement to care or the hospital's ongoing duty of care, and it must never be used to refuse a patient who re-presents.
explanations.B: Leaving against advice is a decision by a person with capacity, often for reasons such as caring responsibilities. The duty of care continues: the team should welcome his return, offer oral therapy or hospital-in-the-home if clinically reasonable, arrange review, and involve the Aboriginal Liaison Officer to address the barriers that led him to leave.
explanations.C: Conditions such as mandatory readmission or an all-or-nothing treatment plan are not legal requirements and are likely to drive him away again; a negotiated plan is safer.
explanations.D: The Mental Health Act 2009 (SA) applies only where a person appears to have a mental illness and meets the criteria for an inpatient treatment order; refusing medical treatment for an infection is not grounds for detention.

learning_point: A discharge against medical advice form does not end the patient's entitlement to care; the team should actively offer a plan the patient can accept and make return easy.
learning_area: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

generation.uncertainty_note: Local health network discharge-against-advice policies differ in wording but all preserve the duty of care and the patient's right to return.

references.title: Medical Board of Australia, Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia
references.locator: Sections 3.3 (informed consent, right to refuse) and 4.7 (cultural safety)

references.title: Australian Charter of Healthcare Rights (2nd edition)

tutor_context: Key facts: Aboriginal patients leave hospital against advice at several times the rate of non-Indigenous patients, often because of family obligations, feeling unsafe or poor communication; this is a system problem to address, not a patient failing. Good practice on discharge against advice includes offering medications and follow-up, documenting capacity and the discussion, and notifying the Aboriginal Liaison Officer. Common misconception: that the signed form transfers all responsibility to the patient. Out of scope: criteria for a Mental Health Act inpatient treatment order.
plan: Tests recall that duty of care and the patient's entitlement to care continue after a discharge against advice (outcomes 1.3, 2.1, 3.6). Scene is a telehealth follow-up call from a metropolitan ward to a young Aboriginal man with carer responsibilities. Distractors: form ends duty, conditional readmission, misuse of the Mental Health Act. Supported by Good medical practice and the Australian Charter of Healthcare Rights.

stem: You are the intern in the emergency department of a metropolitan general hospital, with the medical registrar on site overnight. A 36-year-old Aboriginal man has presented with two hours of central chest pain. His ECG shows ST depression in the lateral leads and the registrar has told you he will be admitted for serial troponins and likely angiography. When you return to explain the plan, he says he wants his aunty, who raised him and has just arrived in the waiting room, to be with him and part of any decisions. His wife is at home with their children and he has not asked for her to be called. He is alert, with capacity, and in no distress.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Explain that only his wife, as legal next of kin, can be involved in discussions about his care
Explain that hospital policy limits clinical discussions to the patient alone while he is in the emergency department
Delay the discussion until the social worker has clarified the family structure in the morning
Ask him whom he would like involved and, with his consent, bring his aunty in to join the discussion of the plan

explanations.A: A patient with capacity chooses who is involved in his care; the "next of kin" concept has no legal force here and does not override his wishes. In many Aboriginal families an aunty or grandmother has a central role regardless of the formal relationship.
explanations.B: No such policy exists, and inventing one damages trust at the moment he most needs support; family presence is usually possible in an emergency department cubicle.
explanations.C: Delaying a straightforward request until business hours leaves him without support during a frightening admission; the social worker is not needed to honour his choice.
explanations.D: Asking who he wants involved respects his autonomy and kinship structure, supports culturally safe care and improves understanding of the plan. The patient's consent to share information is what matters, and it should be documented.

learning_point: Ask Aboriginal patients who they want involved in their care and include those people with the patient's consent, whatever the formal family relationship.
learning_area: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

references.title: Medical Board of Australia, Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia
National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards, User guide for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

tutor_context: Key facts: kinship structures in Aboriginal families often place decision-making support with extended family; a competent adult decides who is involved and what is shared. The legal substitute decision-maker hierarchy only applies when capacity is lost. Common misconception: that a spouse must be consulted first. Out of scope: acute coronary syndrome management.
plan: Tests the basic management step of asking who the patient wants involved and honouring it (outcomes 1.3, 3.6, 1.2). Scene is an emergency department with a man with a non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome asking for his aunty. Distractors are rigid next-of-kin, invented policy and unnecessary delay. Supported by Good medical practice and the ACSQHC Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander user guide.

stem: You are the junior doctor on the medical ward of a country hospital in South Australia, 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre, covering the ward and emergency department overnight with the GP on call by phone. A 79-year-old Aboriginal man with severe COPD and a hip fracture awaiting transfer has become hypoxic and delirious and cannot currently take part in decisions about escalation of his care. He has no advance care directive and no appointed guardian. Six family members are present; a man introduced as his nephew says he has always been the one who speaks for the old man and makes decisions with him, and that the patient's only daughter lives in Adelaide and has had little contact for years. You need to decide who can lawfully consent on his behalf.
lead_in: Which statement is correct under South Australian law?

options.text: A relative by Aboriginal kinship with a close and continuing relationship with him can be the person responsible
Only his daughter, as his closest blood relative, can give consent, and she must be contacted before any decision
The South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal must appoint a guardian before any medical decision can be made
Decisions about limiting treatment cannot be made by family at all and rest solely with the treating consultant

explanations.A: The Consent to Medical Treatment and Palliative Care Act 1995 (SA) sets out who may consent for an adult without capacity: a substitute decision-maker under an advance care directive, a guardian, then a prescribed relative, then an adult friend or carer. A relative includes a person related by blood, marriage, adoption or Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander kinship rules who has a close and continuing relationship with the patient, so the nephew can be the person responsible.
explanations.B: Blood proximity does not decide the matter; the Act requires a close and continuing relationship, and an estranged daughter does not automatically outrank a nephew who has acted for him for years.
explanations.C: Tribunal involvement is reserved for disputes or situations with no suitable person responsible; the Act is designed to allow decisions by family without a tribunal order.
explanations.D: The person responsible can consent to or refuse treatment on the patient's behalf, guided by what the patient would have wanted; emergency treatment to save life can proceed without consent, but the family's role in limitation decisions remains.

learning_point: In South Australia, a relative under Aboriginal kinship rules with a close and continuing relationship can be the person responsible for consent when there is no advance care directive or guardian.
setting_note: Overnight in a country hospital the junior doctor should phone the GP on call before any limitation decision, but can confidently involve the nephew as the person responsible rather than delaying while trying to reach a distant relative.
learning_area: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health
secondary_areas: Palliative care and goals of care

generation.uncertainty_note: Confident that the SA Act recognises Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander kinship relationships within the person-responsible hierarchy; reviewers should confirm the current section numbering.

references.title: Consent to Medical Treatment and Palliative Care Act 1995 (SA) and SA Health Consent to Medical Treatment and Health Care Policy
Advance Care Directives Act 2013 (SA)

tutor_context: Key facts: SA hierarchy is advance care directive substitute decision-maker, then guardian, then prescribed relative (spouse or domestic partner, adult related by blood, marriage, adoption or Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander kinship rules, with a close and continuing relationship), then adult friend or carer. Decisions must reflect what the patient would have wanted. Emergency life-saving treatment can be given without consent. Common misconception: that next of kin is a legal status based on closeness of blood relationship. Out of scope: process for SACAT guardianship applications.
plan: Tests recall of the SA person-responsible hierarchy and its explicit recognition of Aboriginal kinship (outcomes 1.3, 1.2, 2.1). Scene is a country hospital overnight with a delirious elderly man and family present. Distractors: blood-proximity next of kin, mandatory tribunal, consultant-only decisions. Supported by the Consent to Medical Treatment and Palliative Care Act 1995 (SA).

stem: You are the intern in the emergency department of a metropolitan general hospital on an afternoon shift, with the registrar available. A 52-year-old Aboriginal man has had a forearm laceration sutured and is ready to go home. His observations show blood pressure 168/98 mmHg on two readings, he has a body mass index of 34, smokes 15 cigarettes a day and mentions that his father had a heart attack at 50. He says he has not seen a doctor for "years", does not have a regular GP, and that scripts are expensive so he usually does not fill them. He is asymptomatic and his ECG is normal. The hospital's Aboriginal Liaison Officer is on duty.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action to address his longer-term health?

options.text: Prescribe amlodipine on a hospital script and advise him to see a GP at some point in the future for review
Refer him to the hospital's cardiology outpatient clinic for a specialist assessment of his hypertension
Link him to an Aboriginal health service or GP for a health assessment and Closing the Gap PBS registration
Admit him under the general medical team for further investigation and control of his blood pressure

explanations.A: Starting an antihypertensive from the emergency department without follow-up, for a man who says he cannot afford scripts and has no GP, is unlikely to achieve anything and may expose him to unmonitored side effects.
explanations.B: Uncomplicated hypertension does not need a specialist clinic; it needs continuity of primary care where his overall cardiovascular risk, smoking and weight can be managed over time.
explanations.C: He has multiple cardiovascular risk factors and the main barrier is access to affordable primary care. The Medicare health assessment for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people (item 715) is the entry point to structured risk management, and registration for the Closing the Gap PBS co-payment measure, which is done through a general practice or Aboriginal health service, removes or reduces the cost of his medicines. The Aboriginal Liaison Officer can make the connection and a warm referral far more likely to succeed.
explanations.D: Asymptomatic hypertension without end-organ damage is not an indication for admission; it would use an acute bed without solving his lack of ongoing care.

learning_point: For an Aboriginal patient without primary care, the most useful emergency department intervention for chronic disease risk is a warm referral to an Aboriginal health service or GP for a health assessment and Closing the Gap PBS registration.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the Aboriginal health team or local Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service plays the same role; the intern may need to phone the service directly.
learning_area: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health
presentation: health assessment and Closing the Gap PBS

generation.uncertainty_note: Closing the Gap PBS registration is by a GP, Aboriginal health service or other eligible practice; since 2021 any PBS prescriber, including hospital doctors, may write CTG-annotated scripts for a registered patient, but this man is not yet registered.

references.title: Department of Health and Aged Care, Closing the Gap PBS Co-payment Program and MBS item 715 (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Assessment)
RACGP National guide to preventive healthcare for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people (4th edition)

tutor_context: Key facts: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are eligible for an annual 715 health assessment from birth; absolute cardiovascular risk assessment is recommended from age 30 (and from 18 in some guidance). Closing the Gap PBS co-payment registration is a one-off registration through a practice; hospital doctors cannot register patients but can prescribe CTG scripts once registered. Common misconception: that the emergency department's job ends at the acute problem. Out of scope: antihypertensive selection.
plan: Tests management of an incidental chronic disease risk profile in an Aboriginal man without primary care, focusing on the health assessment and Closing the Gap PBS measure (outcomes 1.3, 3.1, 4.4). Scene is an ED discharge with an ALO available. Distractors: unsupported prescribing, inappropriate specialist referral, unnecessary admission. Supported by the RACGP National guide and DoHAC program information.

stem: You are the intern in the emergency department of a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. A 34-year-old Aboriginal woman from the APY Lands, whose first language is Pitjantjatjara and who speaks limited English, has presented with 12 hours of right lower abdominal pain. She is haemodynamically stable with localised tenderness. The surgical registrar has reviewed her and asks you to obtain consent for a CT abdomen and, depending on the result, an appendicectomy, and to do this quickly because the CT slot is in 30 minutes. Her 12-year-old son, who speaks English well, has been translating so far. The Aboriginal Liaison Officer is on site, and the hospital has access to telephone and video interpreting services.
lead_in: What is the most important step to take before the consent discussion?

options.text: Proceed with her son interpreting, since he has already been doing so and time matters
Book a Pitjantjatjara interpreter through the telephone or video interpreting service
Ask the Aboriginal Liaison Officer to interpret the consent discussion for her
Ask a ward nurse who speaks some Pitjantjatjara to explain the procedure to her

explanations.A: Children must not be used as interpreters for clinical decisions: it places an unfair burden on the child, risks inaccurate translation of medical content and compromises her privacy. Her condition is stable and a short delay to arrange an interpreter is safe.
explanations.B: Valid consent requires that she understands the nature, risks and alternatives of the procedure in a language she commands. An accredited interpreter (the Interpreting and Translating Centre or the national service) provides this, and the Aboriginal Liaison Officer can support her, help with family contact and cultural safety, but does not replace the interpreter. Pitjantjatjara interpreters are limited, so the request should be made now.
explanations.C: Aboriginal Liaison Officers provide cultural and practical support; unless they are an accredited interpreter in the relevant language they should not be used to interpret clinical consent, and asking them to do so blurs their role.
explanations.D: Partial language skills in a staff member are not adequate for consent to surgery; misunderstanding of risks or alternatives is likely.

learning_point: Consent for an investigation or operation in a patient with limited English requires an accredited interpreter; family members, children and Aboriginal Liaison Officers should not interpret clinical consent.
learning_area: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

references.title: SA Health Consent to Medical Treatment and Health Care Policy and SA Health Interpreter Services guideline
references.locator: Use of accredited interpreters for consent

references.title: National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards (2nd edition)
references.locator: Partnering with Consumers Standard, Action 2.6 and 2.8

tutor_context: Key facts: an accredited interpreter should be used for any significant clinical communication, especially consent, when the patient is not proficient in English; in SA this is through the Interpreting and Translating Centre or the national Translating and Interpreting Service, with Aboriginal language interpreters available via specialist services. Children and relatives should not interpret except in a life-threatening emergency when no alternative exists. Common misconception: that the Aboriginal Liaison Officer is an interpreter. Out of scope: imaging choice in suspected appendicitis.
plan: Tests prioritisation of arranging an accredited interpreter over expediency when consent is needed (outcomes 1.3, 1.2, 2.8). Scene is a tertiary ED with a stable Pitjantjatjara-speaking woman and a son translating. Distractors: use the child, use the ALO as interpreter, use a part-speaking nurse. Supported by SA Health consent and interpreter policies and NSQHS Partnering with Consumers actions.

stem: You are the PGY2 covering the ward and the emergency department overnight at a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre, with the GP on call by phone. At 02:00 the nurse tells you a 29-year-old Aboriginal woman has arrived with abdominal pain, triaged category 4. The nurse adds, "She's back again, third time this fortnight, the notes say drug-seeking." Her previous two visits ended with analgesia and discharge without investigations; the notes record no examination findings. Her observations tonight are heart rate 108 beats per minute, temperature 37.9 degrees Celsius, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg. You have one other patient, a man with stable chest pain awaiting a repeat troponin in an hour.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate priority?

options.text: Review her previous notes, offer analgesia as on earlier visits and discharge her with advice to see the GP
Ask the nurse to contact the GP on call to see her in the morning so you can focus on the chest pain patient
Request a urine drug screen before deciding whether analgesia is appropriate for her tonight
Assess her now as a new presentation, with a full history, examination and relevant investigations

explanations.A: Repeating the earlier approach anchors on a label that was never supported by documented assessment; repeat presentations with tachycardia and low-grade fever raise the likelihood of a missed diagnosis such as pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy or appendicitis.
explanations.B: Deferring a febrile, tachycardic patient to the morning is not safe; the chest pain patient is stable and awaiting a timed test, so she can and should be seen now.
explanations.C: A drug screen does not help diagnose abdominal pain and signals that the clinician has already decided the presentation is not genuine; it entrenches bias and delays care.
explanations.D: Labels such as "drug-seeking" in the records of Aboriginal patients are a recognised form of systemic bias and are associated with under-investigation and worse outcomes. Her repeated attendance and abnormal observations demand a complete assessment, including pregnancy test and bloods, as for any patient, and an honest documented plan.

learning_point: Repeat presentations with abnormal observations require a full fresh assessment; prior labels such as "drug-seeking" are a risk factor for missed diagnosis, not a diagnosis.
setting_note: In a country hospital the junior doctor is often the only clinician who can break a cycle of unexamined repeat presentations; if serious pathology is suspected, early discussion with the GP on call and the tertiary surgical or gynaecology registrar about transfer is appropriate.
learning_area: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

references.title: Medical Board of Australia, Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia
references.locator: Section 4.7 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health and cultural safety; section 2.1 providing good care

references.title: National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards, User guide for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

tutor_context: Key facts: institutional racism manifests as lower rates of investigation, analgesia and admission for Aboriginal patients with the same presentations; frequent presentation is a red flag for an unmet need. Judgemental labels in notes propagate through episodes. Common misconception: that prior attendances without a diagnosis make serious disease less likely. Out of scope: the differential diagnosis workup itself.
plan: Tests prioritisation: seeing a labelled, frequently attending Aboriginal woman with abnormal observations now and assessing her afresh (outcomes 3.4, 1.4, 2.8). Scene is a country ED at night with a competing but stable patient. Distractors: repeat prior pattern, defer to GP in the morning, drug screen first. Supported by Good medical practice and the ACSQHC Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander user guide.

stem: You are the resident in the emergency department of a large metropolitan teaching hospital with on-site intensive care, interventional cardiology and 24-hour imaging. A 68-year-old Aboriginal woman from Ceduna has been diagnosed with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction and is pain free on treatment. The cardiology registrar plans angiography tomorrow. She is distressed, says she does not trust hospitals since her husband died in one, and wants to go home to her family on the first flight. Her daughter is 800 kilometres away and she has no family in Adelaide. The cardiology registrar asks you to "get the ALO to sort it out". An Aboriginal Liaison Officer is available on call this evening.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate way to involve the Aboriginal Liaison Officer?

options.text: Ask the Aboriginal Liaison Officer to meet her now, help her contact family and join the angiography discussion
Ask the Aboriginal Liaison Officer to obtain her consent for the angiogram so cardiology can proceed in the morning
Ask the Aboriginal Liaison Officer to convince her to stay in hospital until the angiogram has been done
Defer involving the Aboriginal Liaison Officer until the morning ward round, when the registrar can brief them

explanations.A: The Aboriginal Liaison Officer's role is cultural support, advocacy, family contact and helping the clinical team communicate in a way the patient finds safe. Involving them early, with a clear request, gives her the best chance of feeling safe enough to stay, while consent and clinical explanation remain the doctor's responsibility.
explanations.B: Consent must be obtained by a clinician who can explain the procedure, its risks and alternatives; delegating it to the liaison officer is invalid and places them in an inappropriate position.
explanations.C: Asking the liaison officer to persuade or pressure her undermines their trust relationship with the patient and misunderstands their role; she has capacity and the decision is hers.
explanations.D: Her distress and her wish to leave are present now, and the first flight leaves before the ward round; waiting overnight risks a preventable departure with an untreated myocardial infarction.

learning_point: Involve the Aboriginal Liaison Officer early and with a clear request for support and advocacy, not as a substitute for the doctor's duties of explanation and consent or as a persuader.
setting_note: A tertiary hospital usually has an on-call Aboriginal Liaison Officer or Aboriginal Health Practitioner after hours; in a regional hospital the resident may instead call the Aboriginal health team by phone or the patient's own Aboriginal health service, and should ask the patient who she would like contacted.
learning_area: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

generation.uncertainty_note: After-hours Aboriginal Liaison Officer availability varies by hospital; the stem states one is on call.

references.title: SA Health Aboriginal Health Care Framework and local health network Aboriginal Liaison Officer role statements
references.locator: Role of Aboriginal Liaison Officers and Aboriginal Patient Pathway Officers

references.title: National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards, User guide for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

tutor_context: Key facts: Aboriginal Liaison Officers and Aboriginal Health Practitioners support patients and families, advocate, help with accommodation and travel (including the Patient Assistance Transport Scheme) and help clinicians communicate; they do not interpret, consent or persuade. Early notification of every Aboriginal admission is expected. Common misconception: that a referral to the liaison officer transfers responsibility for the patient's engagement. Out of scope: timing and indications for invasive management of NSTEMI.
plan: Tests nuanced management of how to use the Aboriginal Liaison Officer when a patient with an acute coronary syndrome wants to leave (outcomes 1.3, 2.5, 3.6). Scene is a tertiary ED with an on-call ALO and a registrar who wants the problem handed off. Distractors: ALO obtains consent, ALO persuades, defer to morning. Supported by SA Health ALO role guidance and the ACSQHC user guide.

stem: You are the intern at a regional hospital with a small medical ward and no intensive care unit, making a telehealth follow-up call one week after discharge to a 79-year-old woman who was admitted with an exacerbation of COPD. She is recovering well on her usual inhalers and lives independently in a town 40 minutes away. She asks about vaccinations because her neighbour "caught shingles and was in agony". You confirm from the Australian Immunisation Register that she received this year's influenza vaccine and her COVID-19 booster in the last six months, but there is no record of pneumococcal or zoster vaccination. She has no history of immunosuppression and no allergies, and is happy to see her GP.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Reassure her that the influenza and COVID-19 vaccines are the only vaccines recommended at her age
Advise that pneumococcal vaccination is unlikely to benefit her now that she is over 75 years of age
Recommend she see her GP for funded pneumococcal and two-dose recombinant zoster vaccination
Advise against the zoster vaccine because inhaled corticosteroids make a live vaccine unsafe

explanations.A: The Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends several additional vaccines for older adults, including pneumococcal and zoster vaccination, and an admission for COPD is a good prompt to catch up.
explanations.B: Adults aged 70 years and over without prior pneumococcal vaccination are recommended and funded to receive it; COPD further increases her risk of pneumococcal pneumonia and invasive disease.
explanations.C: The Handbook recommends pneumococcal vaccination for all adults from 70 years, and the recombinant zoster vaccine (two doses, 2 to 6 months apart) for adults from 65 years; both are funded on the National Immunisation Program for her. Her GP can give them and record them on the Australian Immunisation Register.
explanations.D: The recombinant zoster vaccine is not a live vaccine and is safe with inhaled corticosteroids; the earlier live zoster vaccine is no longer in use in Australia.

learning_point: A hospital contact with an older adult is an opportunity to check the Australian Immunisation Register and recommend funded pneumococcal and recombinant zoster vaccination.

generation.uncertainty_note: The exact pneumococcal vaccine product and schedule for adults aged 70 and over has been revised more than once; the item deliberately refers to pneumococcal vaccination generically and the GP should apply the current Handbook schedule.

references.title: Australian Immunisation Handbook
references.locator: Pneumococcal disease; Zoster (herpes zoster); Vaccination for older adults

tutor_context: Key facts: National Immunisation Program funds pneumococcal vaccination for non-Indigenous adults from 70 years (from 50 years for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults) and recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix, two doses) from 65 years (from 50 years for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults and for immunocompromised adults from 18). Respiratory syncytial virus vaccination is also recommended from 75 years. Common misconception: that zoster vaccine is live and contraindicated with steroids. Out of scope: COVID-19 booster intervals.
plan: Tests management of adult immunisation catch-up in an older woman after a COPD admission (outcomes 3.1, 3.2). Scene is a telehealth call from a regional hospital with the Immunisation Register checked. Distractors: nothing more needed, too old to benefit, live-vaccine fear. Supported by the Australian Immunisation Handbook pneumococcal and zoster chapters.

stem: You are the intern in the outpatient clinic of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, seeing patients before the visiting surgeon's list. A 38-year-old man who farms near the town is being worked up for elective inguinal hernia repair. In the pre-admission questionnaire he reports drinking six to eight stubbies of full-strength beer on four nights a week and his AUDIT-C score is 8 out of 12. He has never had withdrawal symptoms, seizures or blackouts, does not drink in the morning and has had no injuries or legal problems related to alcohol. His gamma-glutamyl transferase is 92 U/L and other liver tests are normal. He says "everyone around here drinks like that".
lead_in: Which interpretation of his drinking is most accurate?

options.text: He has alcohol dependence and will require inpatient withdrawal management before his surgery can be scheduled
He is drinking at a risky level above Australian guidelines, warranting brief intervention and withdrawal planning
His intake is within the Australian guideline of no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no action is needed
His raised gamma-glutamyl transferase indicates established alcoholic liver disease needing hepatology referral first

explanations.A: Dependence is defined by features such as tolerance, withdrawal, loss of control and continued use despite harm; he reports none of these, so inpatient withdrawal management is not indicated, although peri-operative monitoring for withdrawal is sensible.
explanations.B: Six to eight full-strength stubbies is about 8 to 11 standard drinks per occasion and 30 to 45 per week, far above the National Health and Medical Research Council guideline of no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day. An AUDIT-C of 8 indicates risky drinking. A brief intervention using feedback, advice and goal-setting is effective at this level and the anaesthetist should know about his intake.
explanations.C: This misreads the guideline; his weekly intake is three to four times the recommended maximum and his per-occasion intake exceeds the daily limit each time he drinks.
explanations.D: An isolated mildly raised gamma-glutamyl transferase is a marker of heavy drinking, not of established liver disease; with normal other liver tests it does not warrant specialist referral or delay of surgery.

learning_point: Six to eight full-strength beers four nights a week is risky drinking well above the Australian guideline, warranting a brief intervention and peri-operative withdrawal planning, not a dependence label.
setting_note: In a regional town with high local drinking norms, framing the discussion around the guideline numbers and his own goals is more effective than moral judgement; the local drug and alcohol service and the national Alcohol and Drug Information Service (1300 13 1340 in SA) can provide follow-up support.

references.title: National Health and Medical Research Council, Australian guidelines to reduce health risks from drinking alcohol (2020)
Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction
references.locator: Screening for alcohol use; brief intervention

tutor_context: Key facts: a full-strength 375 mL stubby is about 1.4 standard drinks; AUDIT-C of 4 or more in men (3 in women) suggests risky drinking, higher scores are more concerning but do not by themselves diagnose dependence. Brief intervention (FLAGS: feedback, listen, advice, goals, strategies) is effective in non-dependent risky drinkers. Pre-operatively, heavy drinkers have higher complication rates and may need withdrawal monitoring and thiamine. Common misconception: that any heavy drinker is dependent, or that normal transaminases exclude a drinking problem. Out of scope: pharmacotherapy for alcohol dependence.
plan: Tests interpretation of an AUDIT-C score and quantity of drinking against the NHMRC guideline, distinguishing risky drinking from dependence (outcomes 3.1, 3.2, 1.4). Scene is a regional surgical pre-admission clinic. Distractors: dependence requiring detox, within guideline, liver disease. Supported by NHMRC 2020 guidelines and Therapeutic Guidelines Addiction.

stem: You are the intern on a general practice rotation linked to a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula, where the 4-bed emergency department is staffed overnight by one junior doctor with the GP on call. A 68-year-old woman attends for repeat prescriptions. She has had chronic low back pain for eight years and takes modified-release oxycodone 20 mg twice daily, pregabalin 150 mg twice daily and diazepam 5 mg at night, all prescribed by a GP who has since left the practice. Her MRI two years ago showed degenerative change only. She mentions she feels drowsy most mornings, has had two falls in the past month, one with a wrist sprain, and that her daughter has stopped letting her mind the grandchildren. She would like the scripts renewed today as she is "nearly out". The supervising GP is available between patients.
lead_in: Which issue is the most important to address at this visit?

options.text: Renew the three prescriptions as she has requested today and book her a routine review in three months
Arrange a repeat MRI of her lumbar spine to look for a new, potentially surgical cause of her pain
Refer her to the multidisciplinary pain clinic in Adelaide and continue the current medications until she is seen
Address the sedation and falls from her opioid, benzodiazepine and gabapentinoid, planning a supervised taper

explanations.A: Continuing an unchanged regimen that is already causing falls, daytime sedation and loss of function is unsafe; an intern should not simply renew high-risk scripts inherited from a departed prescriber without review.
explanations.B: There is no new neurological deficit or red flag; repeat imaging for chronic low back pain with known degenerative change does not change management and may reinforce a structural model of her pain.
explanations.C: Pain clinic referral is reasonable later, but waits are long and the immediate harm from her current combination of sedatives must be dealt with now rather than left in place for months.
explanations.D: The combination of an opioid, a benzodiazepine and a gabapentinoid in a 68-year-old is the most likely cause of her falls, drowsiness and loss of role; these harms outweigh any benefit for chronic non-cancer pain. Checking ScriptCheckSA, discussing goals with her, and planning a gradual supervised reduction with the GP, with non-drug strategies and regular review, is the priority.

learning_point: In an older patient on an opioid, benzodiazepine and gabapentinoid with falls and sedation, the priority is to address the combination and plan a supervised taper, not to renew or image.
setting_note: Rural practices often inherit long-standing opioid regimens from previous prescribers; the Adelaide pain clinic and drug and alcohol services offer telehealth support for tapering, and the Rural Support Service can help with case conferencing.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic
references.locator: Chronic non-cancer pain; opioid deprescribing; drugs that cause sedation in combination

references.title: SA Health ScriptCheckSA real-time prescription monitoring and Drugs of Dependence Unit guidance

tutor_context: Key facts: opioids provide little long-term benefit for chronic non-cancer pain and combination with benzodiazepines and gabapentinoids markedly increases sedation, falls and respiratory depression; falls in older people on sedatives are a trigger for deprescribing. ScriptCheckSA must be checked before prescribing monitored drugs in SA; ongoing Schedule 8 prescribing beyond two months requires Drugs of Dependence Unit authority. Taper gradually (for example 10 to 25 percent every 1 to 4 weeks) with support. Common misconception: that the patient must stop everything immediately, or that imaging will reveal a fixable cause. Out of scope: exact taper schedule and pregabalin dosing.
plan: Tests prioritisation in a GP clinic: recognising that polypharmacy harm (falls, sedation) outranks script renewal, imaging or deferred referral (outcomes 3.2, 1.8, 3.6). Scene is a Yorke Peninsula practice with an available supervising GP. Distractors: renew, MRI, pain clinic with no interim action. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Analgesic and SA ScriptCheckSA requirements.

stem: You are the intern in the general medicine outpatient clinic of a large metropolitan teaching hospital, seeing a new patient before presenting to the consultant. A 34-year-old Aboriginal woman has been referred by her GP for "weight management". Her body mass index is 38, blood pressure 142/90 mmHg, HbA1c 6.2 percent, lipids mildly raised and she has no symptoms. She works full time, has two children and tells you that she and her partner hope to have another baby in the next year. She has tried several diets without lasting success and asks whether "the injections" or surgery would be best for her. She attends an Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service for her general care.
lead_in: Which issue should be addressed first?

options.text: Discuss her pregnancy plans and agree preconception care alongside lifestyle weight management
Start a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist to achieve weight loss before she conceives
Refer her for bariatric surgery assessment, given her body mass index and metabolic risk factors
Advise her to postpone pregnancy until she has reduced her body mass index to below 30

explanations.A: Her plan to conceive within a year changes everything: it rules out drug and surgical options that require effective contraception and a delay to pregnancy, and it makes preconception care (folate, optimising glucose and blood pressure, lifestyle support) the most valuable and time-sensitive intervention. Shared decision-making with her and continuity through her Aboriginal health service give the plan the best chance of success.
explanations.B: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists are not recommended in pregnancy and must be stopped well before conception; starting one in a woman planning pregnancy within a year offers little and risks exposure.
explanations.C: Bariatric surgery requires 12 to 18 months of avoiding pregnancy afterwards and lifelong nutritional follow-up; it is incompatible with her stated plan and should not be the first step.
explanations.D: Telling her to delay pregnancy until she reaches a body mass index target is paternalistic, may not be achievable, and ignores her priorities; the task is to make her planned pregnancy as healthy as possible.

learning_point: When a woman with obesity plans pregnancy, preconception care takes priority over pharmacological and surgical weight-loss options that require pregnancy to be delayed.
secondary_areas: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

references.title: RACGP National guide to preventive healthcare for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people (4th edition)
Therapeutic Guidelines: Diabetes (and Obesity)
references.locator: Pharmacotherapy for obesity; use in pregnancy

tutor_context: Key facts: obesity in pregnancy increases gestational diabetes, hypertensive disorders and congenital anomaly risk, and preconception optimisation helps; higher-dose folate (5 mg) is recommended for women with body mass index over 30. Semaglutide and tirzepatide require cessation before conception; bariatric surgery requires delaying pregnancy. Common misconception: that the most potent weight-loss intervention is always the first priority. Out of scope: detailed obstetric management.
plan: Tests prioritisation where a reproductive plan determines which chronic disease interventions are appropriate (outcomes 3.1, 3.6, 1.3). Scene is a tertiary outpatient clinic with a young Aboriginal woman planning pregnancy. Distractors: GLP-1 agonist, bariatric referral, delay pregnancy. Supported by the RACGP National guide and Therapeutic Guidelines.

stem: You are the PGY2 at a regional hospital with a small medical ward and no intensive care unit, making a telehealth follow-up call to a 66-year-old man discharged last week after treatment for community-acquired pneumonia. He has recovered well. During the call he mentions that a bowel screening kit arrived in the post, that he sent it off about two months ago and received a letter saying the result was "positive" and that he should see his GP. He has not done so because he feels well, has no change in bowel habit, no weight loss and "has always had a bit of a haemorrhoid". He has no family history of bowel cancer and has never had a colonoscopy. His haemoglobin on admission was 138 g/L.
lead_in: Which interpretation of his screening result is most accurate?

options.text: It is most likely a false positive from his haemorrhoid and he can safely wait for the next kit in two years
It indicates a meaningful chance of cancer or advanced adenoma, and he needs prompt colonoscopy referral
It means he has bowel cancer and should be referred directly to a colorectal surgeon for staging
The test is unreliable in people over 65 years and should be repeated before any further action

explanations.A: Haemorrhoids can cause a positive result, but they cannot be assumed to be the cause; among participants with a positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test roughly 1 in 30 has cancer and a substantial proportion have advanced adenomas, and a normal haemoglobin does not exclude either.
explanations.B: The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program recommends colonoscopy, ideally within 120 days of a positive result, because early-stage cancer and adenomas are usually asymptomatic. Absence of symptoms is expected in a screening population and provides no reassurance. His GP can arrange the referral and the program follows up non-attendance.
explanations.C: A positive faecal immunochemical test is a screening result, not a diagnosis; most positives are not cancer, and the next step is diagnostic colonoscopy rather than surgical referral.
explanations.D: The program screens people aged 45 to 74 and the test performs well across this range; repeating the kit after a positive result delays diagnosis and is not recommended.

learning_point: A positive bowel screening test needs colonoscopy within about four months irrespective of symptoms or a presumed benign cause such as haemorrhoids.
setting_note: In regional South Australia, colonoscopy waits can be long; the GP should refer as a positive screening result (a category 1 referral) so the regional endoscopy list or Adelaide service can prioritise him.

references.title: Cancer Council Australia, Clinical practice guidelines for the prevention, early detection and management of colorectal cancer
references.locator: Population screening; management of a positive iFOBT

references.title: RACGP Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice (Red Book)

tutor_context: Key facts: the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program invites people aged 45 to 74 every two years; a positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test should be followed by colonoscopy within 120 days; positive predictive value for cancer is around 3 to 4 percent and for advanced adenoma around 20 to 30 percent. Common misconception: that symptoms or haemorrhoids explain the result. Out of scope: surveillance intervals after polypectomy.
plan: Tests interpretation of a positive screening iFOBT in an asymptomatic man and the need for colonoscopy (outcomes 3.1, 1.5). Scene is a telehealth call from a regional hospital. Distractors: dismiss as haemorrhoids, overcall as cancer, repeat the kit. Supported by Cancer Council colorectal cancer guidelines and the RACGP Red Book.

stem: You are the intern at a tertiary hospital in Adelaide, conducting a telehealth review for a 55-year-old woman who was discharged a fortnight ago after an admission with a COPD exacerbation. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day, has her first cigarette within five minutes of waking, and says the admission "scared her into" wanting to quit. Two years ago she used a 21 mg nicotine patch alone for three weeks, found the cravings unbearable and relapsed. She has depression that is stable on sertraline 100 mg daily and asks what she should try this time. The respiratory registrar has asked you to make a plan and arrange a prescription through her GP.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.text: Advise that since nicotine replacement has already failed, her best chance is to stop without medication
Recommend bupropion as first-line therapy, because it will also help to treat her depression
Recommend a 21 mg patch plus a fast-acting nicotine product for cravings, with referral to Quitline
Recommend that she switch to a nicotine vaping product as the first-line approach this time

explanations.A: Unaided quitting has the lowest success rate; a previous short course of patch monotherapy is not a reason to abandon pharmacotherapy but to use it properly, in combination and for a full 8 to 12 weeks with behavioural support.
explanations.B: Bupropion is less effective than combination nicotine replacement or varenicline, lowers the seizure threshold, and is not a treatment for her already-stable depression; combining it with sertraline needs specialist consideration and it is not a first-line choice here.
explanations.C: Combination nicotine replacement therapy (a patch for background nicotine plus a fast-acting product for breakthrough cravings) roughly doubles quit rates compared with a patch alone and directly addresses the problem she had last time. Her high dependence (first cigarette within five minutes of waking) supports the 21 mg patch. Both forms are PBS-subsidised, and Quitline multi-session support further improves success. Her depression and sertraline are not contraindications.
explanations.D: Nicotine vaping products are prescription-only in Australia and the RACGP recommends them only after first-line therapies have genuinely failed and with behavioural support; she has not had an adequate trial of first-line therapy.

learning_point: After relapse on a nicotine patch alone, the next step is combination nicotine replacement therapy (patch plus a fast-acting form) with Quitline support, which is safe in stable depression.

generation.uncertainty_note: Varenicline is also a first-line option and was deliberately left out of the options to avoid two defensible answers; its availability in Australia has changed since 2021.

references.title: RACGP, Supporting smoking cessation: a guide for health professionals (2nd edition, updated)
Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction

tutor_context: Key facts: first-line pharmacotherapies are combination nicotine replacement therapy and varenicline; bupropion is second-line. Time to first cigarette under 30 minutes indicates high dependence. Nicotine replacement is PBS-listed (patches and some fast-acting forms) and safe in cardiovascular disease and in people with mental illness. Quitline (13 7848) provides free multi-session behavioural support and callback. Nicotine vaping products are prescription-only and not first-line. Common misconception: that failure on one NRT product means NRT does not work for that patient. Out of scope: varenicline dosing and the status of its PBS listing.
plan: Tests management of smoking cessation after a prior patch failure in a woman with stable depression (outcomes 3.1, 3.2, 1.8). Scene is a tertiary telehealth call. Distractors: unaided quit, bupropion as antidepressant-plus-cessation, vaping first-line. Supported by the RACGP smoking cessation guide and Therapeutic Guidelines Addiction.

stem: You are the PGY2 in the heart failure outpatient clinic of a large metropolitan teaching hospital, with the consultant available. A 58-year-old woman with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction attends for review three weeks after her third admission in six months for fluid overload. She is euvolaemic today on furosemide 40 mg twice daily and standard heart failure therapy. She tells you she lost her rental property two months ago and has been sleeping in her car, that she cannot afford all her medications so takes "the important ones", has no scales, and missed two clinic appointments because she had no fuel. She is not depressed and does not drink alcohol. She has a mobile phone and a Centrelink payment.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase her furosemide dose and book a review in two weeks' time to reduce her chance of readmission
Discharge her from the clinic for her non-attendance and ask her GP to take over managing her heart failure
Refer her to psychiatry for an assessment of her non-adherence before making any changes to her treatment plan
Involve social work today, simplify her regimen in a dose administration aid and link her with community care

explanations.A: Her readmissions are driven by missed doses and the inability to monitor weight, not by an inadequate diuretic dose; increasing the dose without addressing why she cannot take her medicines risks dehydration and renal impairment when she does take them.
explanations.B: Removing her from the clinic penalises her for the circumstances causing her illness and will almost certainly lead to further admissions; non-attendance is a signal to reach out, not to discharge.
explanations.C: Her reasons for missing doses are financial and practical, and she has no features of a mental illness; a psychiatric referral misattributes a social problem and delays practical help.
explanations.D: Housing, cost and transport are the social determinants driving her admissions. Same-day social work involvement can address housing, Centrelink entitlements, medication costs and transport; a simplified regimen in a dose administration aid is cheaper and easier to adhere to; the community heart failure nurse can monitor her by phone and arrange scales; and the PBS Safety Net and concession pricing reduce cost. This is whole-of-person care within a PGY2's remit.

learning_point: When social circumstances drive repeated admissions, the effective intervention is to address them directly (social work, medication cost and simplification, community nursing) rather than adjust doses or discharge the patient.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the same tasks fall to the ward social worker, the local council or community health service and the GP; community heart failure nurses may be available by telehealth from Adelaide.

references.title: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand, Guidelines for the prevention, detection and management of heart failure in Australia (2018)
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care, Acute Coronary Syndromes and chronic condition clinical care standards; NSQHS Comprehensive Care Standard
references.locator: Comprehensive care planning including social needs

tutor_context: Key facts: non-adherence is the leading precipitant of heart failure readmission; multidisciplinary heart failure programs with nurse follow-up reduce admissions; homelessness, cost and transport are modifiable with social work and community services. Dose administration aids and once-daily regimens improve adherence. Common misconception: that adherence problems are attitudinal rather than structural. Out of scope: titration of heart failure pharmacotherapy.
plan: Tests management of social determinants as the cause of repeated admissions (outcomes 3.2, 3.6, 1.7). Scene is a tertiary heart failure clinic with a woman who is homeless and cannot afford medicines. Distractors: dose escalation, discharge for non-attendance, psychiatric referral. Supported by the Heart Foundation heart failure guideline and NSQHS comprehensive care requirements.

stem: You are the intern on a general practice rotation linked to a regional hospital that has a small medical ward without intensive care, CT during business hours only and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. A 41-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes diagnosed four years ago attends for her annual cycle of care review. She takes metformin 1 g twice daily and no other medications. Her results are HbA1c 8.4 percent (68 mmol/mol), eGFR 88 mL/min/1.73 m2, urine albumin-creatinine ratio 4.2 mg/mmol with a repeat of 3.8 mg/mmol three months earlier, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, LDL cholesterol 2.6 mmol/L, body mass index 31 and a normal foot examination. Her retinal screen last year was normal. The supervising GP has asked you to summarise what the results mean before you see her together.
lead_in: Which interpretation of her results is most accurate?

options.text: Her glycaemia is above target and she has persistent moderately increased albuminuria, both needing action
Her results are all at target and her current metformin treatment should simply continue unchanged
An albumin-creatinine ratio of 4.2 mg/mmol is normal for a woman, so only her HbA1c needs attention
She has established diabetic nephropathy with declining kidney function and needs urgent nephrology referral

explanations.A: An HbA1c of 8.4 percent is well above the usual target of 7 percent or less for a young woman on metformin alone, so a second agent is indicated. Two albumin-creatinine ratios above 3.5 mg/mmol (the threshold for women) three months apart confirm persistent moderately increased albuminuria, which raises cardiovascular and renal risk and is an indication to consider an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker and an SGLT2 inhibitor even with normal blood pressure.
explanations.B: Her HbA1c is above target and albuminuria is present; continuing unchanged therapy would miss two opportunities to reduce long-term complications.
explanations.C: The sex-specific threshold for moderately increased albuminuria is 3.5 mg/mmol in women (2.5 in men); both of her results exceed it and the finding is persistent.
explanations.D: Her eGFR is normal and the albuminuria is moderate; this is early diabetic kidney disease to be managed in primary care, and referral criteria such as eGFR below 30, rapid decline or heavy albuminuria are not met.

learning_point: In type 2 diabetes, a persistent urine albumin-creatinine ratio above the sex-specific threshold (3.5 mg/mmol in women) is early kidney disease that warrants renin-angiotensin blockade and review of glucose-lowering therapy.

references.title: RACGP, Management of type 2 diabetes: a handbook for general practice
Therapeutic Guidelines: Diabetes
references.locator: Type 2 diabetes: glycaemic management; diabetic kidney disease

tutor_context: Key facts: general HbA1c target 7 percent or less (53 mmol/mol) for most; albumin-creatinine ratio thresholds 2.5 mg/mmol (men) and 3.5 mg/mmol (women), confirmed on two of three samples; persistent albuminuria indicates ACE inhibitor or ARB and favours SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 agonist as second-line agents for renal and cardiovascular benefit.
