Referral to nephrology is for eGFR under 30, albumin-creatinine ratio over 30 mg/mmol with haematuria, or sustained rapid decline. Common misconception: that normal blood pressure makes renin-angiotensin blockade unnecessary. Out of scope: choice and dosing of the second glucose-lowering agent.
plan: Tests interpretation of an annual diabetes review, in particular recognising sex-specific albuminuria thresholds and an above-target HbA1c (outcomes 3.1, 1.5, 3.2). Scene is a regional general practice with the GP supervising. Distractors: all at target, albuminuria dismissed by wrong threshold, over-called nephropathy. Supported by the RACGP diabetes handbook and Therapeutic Guidelines Diabetes.

stem: You are the junior doctor on the medical ward of a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre, covering the ward and emergency department overnight with the physician on call by phone. A 36-year-old man admitted yesterday with right lower lobe pneumonia on intravenous benzylpenicillin and oral doxycycline has deteriorated: respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 91 percent on 4 L/min via nasal prongs, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, heart rate 118 beats per minute and temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius, which triggers a red-zone response under the Rapid Detection and Response chart. You have started the sepsis pathway, taken cultures, given a 500 mL crystalloid bolus and are about to phone the physician using the ISBAR framework.
lead_in: Which statement belongs in the Recommendation component of your ISBAR call?

options.text: "I am the resident covering the medical ward tonight and I am calling about a patient who is in the red zone."
"I would like you to come in and review him now, and I want to give a second 500 mL bolus while I wait; do you agree?"
"He is a 36-year-old admitted yesterday with right lower lobe pneumonia on intravenous benzylpenicillin and doxycycline."
"His respiratory rate is 28, saturations 91 percent on 4 litres, blood pressure 98 over 60 and heart rate 118."

explanations.A: Identifying yourself, your role and the patient is the Identify component, the opening of the call rather than the request.
explanations.B: The Recommendation is the explicit statement of what you need from the listener and by when, plus what you propose to do in the meantime, and it should end with a check that both parties agree. Stating a clear request (attend now, agreement to a second bolus) is the part most often omitted by junior doctors and the part that most changes the outcome of the call.
explanations.C: The admission diagnosis and current treatment are Background, the context that helps the listener understand the situation.
explanations.D: The observations and the red-zone trigger are part of the Assessment (together with your impression, in this case septic shock until proven otherwise), not the Recommendation.

learning_point: The Recommendation in ISBAR states clearly what you want the senior to do and when, what you propose to do meanwhile, and confirms agreement; it is the component most often left out.
setting_note: In a country hospital the Recommendation should also include an explicit question about escalation beyond the site, for example whether to contact MedSTAR or the tertiary intensive care unit for retrieval advice now rather than after further deterioration.

references.title: SA Health Clinical Handover Policy Directive and ISBAR tools; Rapid Detection and Response observation chart
National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards (2nd edition)
references.locator: Communicating for Safety Standard, Action 6.8; Recognising and Responding to Acute Deterioration Standard

tutor_context: Key facts: ISBAR is Identify, Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation; the recommendation should be specific (what, by whom, by when), include interim actions and a read-back or agreement check. In SA the Rapid Detection and Response chart red zone requires immediate escalation to a medical officer and consideration of a Medical Emergency Response. Common misconception: that reporting observations alone is sufficient. Out of scope: antibiotic escalation for severe pneumonia.
plan: Tests recall of the ISBAR components by asking which statement is the Recommendation (outcomes 1.1, 1.9, 1.2). Scene is a country hospital overnight with a septic patient and the physician by phone. Each distractor is a correctly worded statement from a different ISBAR component, so the item hinges on knowing what Recommendation means. Supported by the SA Health clinical handover directive and NSQHS Communicating for Safety.

stem: You are the intern on an evening cover shift at a tertiary hospital in Adelaide, covering four surgical wards with the surgical registrar in theatre and the consultant at home. At 20:30 a nurse asks you to see a 34-year-old man admitted that morning with epigastric pain and weight loss. His CT abdomen, reported at 19:00 after the day team left, describes a mass in the head of the pancreas with multiple liver lesions suspicious for metastases and recommends oncological referral. He is comfortable, his partner is at the bedside, and he asks you directly: "They said the scan would be back tonight. What did it show?" The admitting team has not yet seen the report.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Tell him the scan was fine for tonight so he can rest, and leave the result for the day team to discuss
Read him the full report, including the likely metastatic cancer, and answer his questions about prognosis
Tell him the scan shows a serious abnormality, ask what he wants to know, and call the registrar tonight
Tell him that you have not seen the report and that results are only discussed on ward rounds

explanations.A: Telling him the scan was fine is a lie that will be discovered the next morning, destroys trust and denies him the chance to prepare or have family present.
explanations.B: Delivering a diagnosis of probable metastatic cancer and prognosis at night, as an intern who has not seen the images, has not discussed the case with the treating team and cannot answer questions about treatment, risks inaccurate or incomplete information and leaves him without a plan; it exceeds an intern's scope.
explanations.C: Honesty does not require dumping every detail. Acknowledging that the result is serious, exploring what he wants to know and when, ensuring he has support, and escalating to the registrar tonight so that a senior clinician can break the news properly (ideally with the consultant's involvement the next morning or sooner) respects his autonomy and stays within an intern's role. Documenting what was said avoids mixed messages.
explanations.D: Deflecting with a false statement or a non-existent rule is dishonest and leaves him anxious and uninformed.

learning_point: When a serious unexpected result arrives after hours, be honest that it is serious, find out what the patient wants to know, escalate to the registrar for a timely senior discussion, and document; neither lie nor break the full news alone.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the senior clinician may be the visiting surgeon or GP by phone; the intern should still phone them that evening so the news is delivered by someone able to discuss next steps, including referral to Adelaide.

generation.uncertainty_note: Some senior clinicians would argue the patient is entitled to the full result immediately; the keyed answer keeps honesty while escalating so that the full discussion is led by someone who can answer treatment questions.

references.title: Medical Board of Australia, Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia
references.locator: Sections 3.2 (good patient care), 3.3 (effective communication) and 2.2 (recognising limits of competence)

references.title: Clinical practice guidelines for communicating prognosis and end-of-life issues (Clayton et al, Medical Journal of Australia 2007) and the SPIKES protocol

tutor_context: Key facts: principles of breaking bad news (setting, perception, invitation, knowledge in small chunks, empathy, strategy) apply even when the full conversation must be deferred; patients have a right to honesty but also to choose how much they hear and when. Interns should escalate rather than deliver major diagnoses alone, and the registrar should be told tonight, not left to find the report tomorrow. Common misconception: that the only choices are lying or telling everything. Out of scope: management of pancreatic cancer.
plan: Tests management of a direct question about a serious result after hours, balancing honesty, the patient's preference and an intern's scope (outcomes 1.2, 2.4, 2.1). Scene is an evening cover shift in a tertiary hospital with the registrar in theatre. Distractors: lie, dump the whole report, deflect with a false rule. Supported by Good medical practice and Australian prognosis-communication guidelines.

stem: You are the intern on an evening cover shift at a tertiary hospital in Adelaide, with the gynaecology registrar available by phone. A 29-year-old woman was admitted this afternoon with pelvic pain; her serum hCG is positive, ultrasound has not yet located the pregnancy, and she is stable with serial hCG planned. On admission she told the day team, and it is documented, that she does not want her parents to know she is pregnant. At 21:00 the ward clerk puts through a call from her mother, who says she is listed as next of kin, is very worried, and wants to know "what is wrong with her and what the tests showed". The patient is awake and has capacity.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Tell her mother the working diagnosis, as she is the recorded next of kin and asking in good faith
Tell her mother that you are unable to give any information at all and then end the call
Ask the gynaecology registrar to return the call so that a more senior doctor can decide what to say
Ask the patient what, if anything, she wants shared, then speak to her mother within those limits

explanations.A: Being named next of kin confers no right to clinical information about an adult with capacity; disclosing the pregnancy against her documented wishes breaches confidentiality and could cause real harm.
explanations.B: A flat refusal is unnecessarily harsh and may itself suggest something serious; with the patient's agreement, reassurance that she is safe can usually be given without breaching confidentiality.
explanations.C: Escalating a routine confidentiality question to the on-call registrar at night is not needed and delays a response; managing this call is within an intern's scope.
explanations.D: The patient controls what is shared. A brief check with her allows a response tailored to her wishes, for example that she is stable and being cared for, or that she will phone her mother herself, and protects the information she asked to keep private. Documenting what was agreed and said protects both patient and staff and informs the day team.

learning_point: Information about an adult patient with capacity is shared with family only to the extent the patient agrees, whatever the next-of-kin field says; check with the patient first and document.

references.title: Medical Board of Australia, Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia
SA Health Privacy Policy Directive and Code of Fair Information Practice
references.locator: Disclosure of personal health information to family

tutor_context: Key facts: confidentiality is owed to the patient; next of kin is an administrative contact, not a legal entitlement to information; disclosure to family requires the patient's consent unless she lacks capacity or an exception applies. Telephone callers cannot be verified, which is a further reason for caution. Common misconception: that family members listed as next of kin have a right to results. Out of scope: management of pregnancy of unknown location.
plan: Tests management of a family phone call where the patient has restricted disclosure (outcomes 1.2, 2.1, 1.10). Scene is an evening cover shift in a tertiary hospital with a possible ectopic pregnancy. Distractors: disclose to next of kin, blanket refusal, unnecessary escalation. Supported by Good medical practice section 3.4 and SA Health privacy directives.

stem: You are the intern on the medical ward of a regional hospital that has a small medical ward without intensive care, CT during business hours only and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. A 56-year-old woman admitted with pneumonia was charted enoxaparin 40 mg once daily for thromboprophylaxis; on checking the chart you find that she received 80 mg this morning because the dose was transcribed incorrectly. She is well, with no bleeding, normal observations and a normal creatinine. You have told the registrar, who agrees no treatment is needed beyond observation, and you have entered the incident in the Safety Learning System. Her husband is at the bedside and asks why the nurses have been "checking on her so much".
lead_in: Which statement correctly describes what open disclosure requires in this situation?

options.text: The patient, and her husband if she wishes, should promptly be told what happened and receive an apology
Disclosure should wait until the root cause analysis is complete so that accurate information can be given
Only the medical director or consultant may disclose the error, so the intern should say nothing yet
The word "sorry" should be avoided in the discussion, because an apology is an admission of liability

explanations.A: The Australian Open Disclosure Framework requires that patients, and with their consent their family, are told about an incident that caused or could have caused harm, as soon as practicable; the discussion includes an apology or expression of regret including the word sorry, a factual explanation, the consequences and what is being done, and the steps to prevent recurrence. A double prophylactic dose with no harm still warrants disclosure.
explanations.B: Waiting for a formal review contradicts the framework's requirement for timely disclosure; initial disclosure gives the known facts and promises further information as it becomes available.
explanations.C: Any clinician involved can and should participate in disclosure; a junior doctor should involve the registrar or consultant and follow the local process, but need not stay silent when the patient or family asks, and a lower-level open disclosure for a minor event can be led by the treating team.
explanations.D: The Civil Liability Act 1936 (SA) provides that an apology or expression of regret does not constitute an admission of liability; saying sorry is expected under the national framework.

learning_point: Open disclosure after a medication error means telling the patient promptly and honestly what happened, saying sorry, explaining consequences and prevention, and involving family as the patient wishes; an apology is not an admission of liability.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the consultant may be off site; the intern and registrar can conduct the initial disclosure of a minor incident and inform the consultant, following the local health network's open disclosure procedure.

references.title: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care, Australian Open Disclosure Framework
references.locator: Elements of open disclosure; apology; timing

references.title: SA Health Open Disclosure Policy Directive; Civil Liability Act 1936 (SA) section 75
references.locator: Apology provisions; lower- and higher-level open disclosure

tutor_context: Key facts: the national framework's elements are open and timely communication, acknowledgement, apology or expression of regret, supporting and meeting the needs of the patient and family, supporting staff, integration with clinical governance, and confidentiality. SA has an apology law (Civil Liability Act 1936, s75) protecting apologies from being admissions. Incidents are reported in the Safety Learning System in SA. Common misconception: that an error without harm need not be disclosed. Out of scope: management of enoxaparin overdose.
plan: Tests recall of the elements of open disclosure after a near-harm medication error, prompted by a family member's question (outcomes 1.1, 1.2, 4.3). Scene is a regional medical ward with the registrar involved and the incident reported. Distractors: wait for analysis, only seniors may disclose, avoid apology. Supported by the Australian Open Disclosure Framework and SA apology law.

stem: You are the intern on an evening cover shift at a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre, where you cover the ward and emergency department overnight. The nurse asks you to finalise the discharge summary for a 38-year-old man leaving on the 06:00 bus tomorrow, before the day team arrives. He was admitted five days ago with community-acquired pneumonia and was found to have new atrial fibrillation; the visiting physician started apixaban 5 mg twice daily and metoprolol 25 mg twice daily, planned an echocardiogram and physician review in four weeks, and a blood culture taken on admission is still reported as "no growth to date". The draft summary written by the day resident reads: "Admitted with pneumonia. Treated with IV antibiotics, improved. Discharged on oral amoxicillin to complete 7 days. GP follow-up."
lead_in: Which deficiency in this draft poses the greatest risk to his safety after discharge?

options.text: It does not include the ward's direct telephone number for the GP to call with any later queries
It omits the atrial fibrillation, its new medicines, the pending culture and planned reviews
The hospital course is too brief and does not describe his daily progress during the admission
It does not list the investigations that returned normal results during his five-day admission

explanations.A: A contact number is helpful but its absence is unlikely on its own to lead to harm; the GP can reach the hospital through the switchboard.
explanations.B: The discharge summary is the main communication to the GP. Omitting a new diagnosis, a new anticoagulant and beta blocker (with the reasons they were started and the intended duration), a result still pending, and specific follow-up actions means the GP may stop or fail to continue the anticoagulant, miss a positive culture and overlook the echocardiogram. Medication changes with reasons, pending results and follow-up responsibilities are the elements most strongly linked to post-discharge harm.
explanations.C: A concise hospital course is acceptable and often preferred; narrative detail matters less than the actionable content.
explanations.D: Normal results are low-yield in a discharge summary; what matters are abnormal and pending results and the actions they require.

learning_point: The critical content of a discharge summary is new diagnoses, every medication started, stopped or changed with the reason, results still pending, and who is responsible for each follow-up action.
setting_note: In a country hospital the discharge summary may be the only handover the GP and the Adelaide physician receive; the intern should also telephone the GP practice if the patient leaves before business hours, and note who will chase the blood culture.

references.title: National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards (2nd edition), Communicating for Safety Standard and National guidelines for on-screen presentation of discharge summaries
references.locator: Actions 6.7 to 6.8; discharge summary core content

references.title: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care, Medication Safety Standard and medication reconciliation at transitions of care

tutor_context: Key facts: the ACSQHC discharge summary core elements include principal and secondary diagnoses, medication list with changes and reasons, pending results and who will follow them up, arranged follow-up and information given to the patient. Medication changes and pending results are the most common sources of post-discharge adverse events. Common misconception: that a long narrative equals a good summary. Out of scope: anticoagulation decisions in atrial fibrillation.
plan: Tests interpretation of a deficient draft discharge summary to identify the omission most linked to harm (outcomes 1.1, 1.10, 1.8). Scene is an evening cover shift in a country hospital with an early-morning discharge. Distractors are minor or cosmetic deficiencies. Supported by the ACSQHC Communicating for Safety and Medication Safety standards.
